ctx: the spoken close — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🫧 Öskjuhlíð & Perlan
en: Every building you will see today is heated by water like that. Iceland does not burn anything to keep warm — it just pumps up what is already hot.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🫧 Öskjuhlíð & Perlan
en: The Lid On The City's Hot Water

ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🫧 Öskjuhlíð & Perlan
en: That dome is a **lid.** Under it sit **six steel tanks**, each **ten metres tall and twenty-three across**, each holding about **four million litres** of water at **eighty degrees** — so Reykjavík can run a bath at seven in the morning.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🫧 Öskjuhlíð & Perlan
en: **Öskjuhlíð** is **61 metres** high and made of **Reykjavíkurgrágrýti** — grey basalt erupted from Mosfellsheiði late in the Ice Age, then scraped smooth by glaciers. About **ten thousand years ago it was an island.** The old shoreline round here sits **42 metres** above today's sea.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🫧 Öskjuhlíð & Perlan
en: From **1913** they blasted the north face out and ran it down to the harbour on a **purpose-built railway** — one of the very few stretches of railway Iceland has ever had. **The stone became the harbour. The hole became the bowling alley.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🫧 Öskjuhlíð & Perlan
en: The **Allies took this hill in 1940** and built all over it once the airfield went into Vatnsmýri in **1941.** It is now **the best-preserved military ground in Reykjavík** — pillboxes, command bunkers, trenches, blast walls, and the floors of hundreds of Nissen huts still in the trees.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🫧 Öskjuhlíð & Perlan
en: The first hot-water tank went up in **1940**, more followed, two more in **1966**, and the lot was **demolished in 1986 to 87** and rebuilt. **Perlan** went on top — architect **Ingimundur Sveinsson**, opened **21 June 1991.** The steel frame does two jobs: it ties the tanks together and it is the dome.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🫧 Öskjuhlíð & Perlan
en: The wood is deliberate. Planting started **after about 1950** on a council scheme, and the tallest conifers now clear **15 metres** — birch, mountain pine, Sitka spruce, Alaska poplar. In a country with almost no forest, somebody had to decide to put one here.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧺 Þvottalaugarnar
en: Why The Main Shopping Street Is Called Laundry Road

ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧺 Þvottalaugarnar
en: Reykjavík's main shopping street is called **Laugavegur.** Everyone translates it as something romantic. It means **the road out to the washing pools** — and they are in that valley, and this is the road.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧺 Þvottalaugarnar
en: Out there are the **Þvottalaugarnar**, hot springs the town did its laundry in. First written down in **1672** by the physician **Þorkell Arngrímsson Vídalín**, who reckoned the water healed people. **By about 1830 nearly every household in Reykjavík was using them.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧺 Þvottalaugarnar
en: Women carried the washing out, boiled it, beat it, and carried it home wet. The town council finally voted in **1885** to build them a proper road, and it was laid in **1886.** That road is **Laugavegur.** By **1900** it was the most populous street in town with over **700 residents** — a laundry track that turned into the high street.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧺 Þvottalaugarnar
en: The name runs the other way from what people assume. The **pool** is the oldest name. **Laugardalur**, **Laugarnes**, **Laugalækur**, **Laugavegur** — all of them are named after the *laug*, not the other way about.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧺 Þvottalaugarnar
en: In **1928** they drilled the first borehole beside the pools and got **87 degree** water. In **1930** they ran a **three kilometre pipe** from there to **Austurbæjarskóli** — **Iceland's first municipal district heating.** By **1937** it warmed 58 houses.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧺 Þvottalaugarnar
en: **The same year the pipe was switched on, 1930, the laundry stopped.** The springs did not run out. They got promoted. There is a sculpture in the valley, **Þvottakonan** by **Ásmundur Sveinsson**, 1958, for the women who made the walk.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🗻 Vífilsfell
en: The Mountain Named After A Slave

ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🗻 Vífilsfell
en: There is a mountain out that window **named after a slave** — and the naming is recorded in Iceland's founding text itself.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🗻 Vífilsfell
en: **Landnámabók** puts it in seven words: ***"við hann er kennt Vífilsfell"*** — the mountain is named for him. **Vífill** was one of **Ingólfur Arnarson's** two slaves, sent along the coast to hunt for his high-seat pillars. **Ingólfur gave Vífill his freedom.** The other one, **Karli**, said they had crossed good country only to settle an outlying headland, and walked off. **Only Vífill was freed** — and only Vífill got a mountain.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🗻 Vífilsfell
en: It is **655 metres**, the highest ground in Kópavogur. And that shelf halfway up is the interesting part.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🗻 Vífilsfell
en: **It is two mountains stacked.** The shelf is a **stapi** — a tuya — móberg built under ice and then capped with lava once the eruption melted through and the meltwater could no longer reach the vent. **The summit above it is a second, younger móberg mountain sitting on top of the first**, from a separate eruption in **probably a different ice age.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🗻 Vífilsfell
en: That younger top sits on a **north-west to south-east fissure**, which is odd. Almost every crack in South Iceland runs **north-east to south-west.** This one is at right angles to the grain of the country.

ctx: bad-weather alternative — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá
en: Weather pivot: "Weather barely touches this river. It comes off an ice cap, so it runs much the same in sun or sleet."

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá
en: And a kilometre or so below the bridge sits **Urriðafoss** — **Iceland's most voluminous waterfall.** Not the tallest, not the most powerful. The most *water*. It is only about **six metres high** and it carries roughly **358 cubic metres a second** — about **1.7 times Dettifoss** up north. Dettifoss is the most **powerful**, which is height times flow, and the two get swapped so often that the University of Iceland has had to correct it in print.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá
en: Every winter the river builds an ice jam here called the **Urriðafosshrönn.** Landsvirkjun's own survey measured up to **40 million cubic metres** of ice and slush, a sheet up to **20 metres thick**, burying the waterfall completely — and in some years it backs up past the bridge we are crossing. Iceland's most voluminous waterfall spends part of most winters entirely out of sight, under its own ice.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá
en: People have wanted to dam it since **1927**, when the poet **Einar Benediktsson's** company Titan won a licence it never found the money to use. The modern version is **Urriðafossvirkjun**, **140 MW**. On **17 February 2026** Alþingi left it in **biðflokkur** — the hold category — while everyone waits to see what the two dams upstream do to the **Þjórsá salmon**, one of Iceland's largest wild stocks at around **ten thousand fish.** Landsvirkjun's own assessment says the falls would run at **10 to 15 cubic metres a second** in winter instead of 350, and it proposes **no mitigation.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌊 Þjórsá
en: One last thing, about the name. **Landnámabók** says Þjórsá is 'bull river' because a settler sailed into the mouth with a bull's head on his prow. Iceland's place-name scholars are not convinced. **Þórhallur Vilmundarson** argued it was originally **Þjótsá** — 'the roaring river' — and the roar it was named for is this one, at Urriðafoss. There is a farm on the bank still called **Þjótandi**, 'the one that roars.'

en: A cold, clear, gravel-poor river that had no salmon, engineered into the best salmon fishery in the country.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🐟 Ægissíðufoss
en: The Best Salmon River In Iceland Is Not A Salmon River

ctx: opening hook line — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🐟 Ægissíðufoss
en: In **2022** this river was **the top-producing salmon fishery in the whole of Iceland** — **5,112 fish.** And before the 1970s it had **essentially no salmon in it at all.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🐟 Ægissíðufoss
en: The **Ytri-Rangá** is a **60 km spring-fed river** rising in Rangárbotnar north of Hekla, running at about **50 cubic metres a second** and barely changing — the springs come out at **4 to 6 degrees** all year, so it does not flood in summer and it does not freeze.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🐟 Ægissíðufoss
en: **And that is exactly why it had no salmon.** The bed is too fine, the water too cold, and salmon fry could never get a grip. **These were trout rivers.** Then people started releasing smolts by the hundred thousand.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🐟 Ægissíðufoss
en: In **1982** they cut a **fish ladder** into this waterfall, and another into Árbæjarfoss upstream in **1985.** Both carry **fish counters**, and the one here is the river's census point. In **2024** it logged **6,400 salmon** going up, from which the river reckoned about **twelve thousand** came in off the sea.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🐟 Ægissíðufoss
en: The state fisheries institute is careful enough about it that **when it publishes Iceland's wild salmon figure, it subtracts these rivers first.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🐟 Ægissíðufoss
en: The falls also mark a line in the ground. The old **interglacial shield lavas** that make up all the flat farmland north of here **stop right at Ægissíðufoss.** Everything past it is younger.

en: the lower falls on the Ytri-Rangá, fish ladder cut in 1982

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss
en: Behind the car park sits **Skógar Museum** — and one gorge along, a **bonus waterfall called Kvernufoss** that almost every coach drives straight past. Then the legend of **Þrasi's treasure** — a settler's gold chest hidden behind the falls. Looters once hooked the chest's iron ring, only for it to **snap off**; that ring hung on the **church door until 1890** and now sits in the museum. The gold, naturally, is still behind the water.
